content: Galbanum is an aromatic gum resin derived from certain Persian plant species, primarily Ferula gummosa (synonym galbaniflura) and Ferula rubricaulis. These plants are abundant on the slopes of the mountain ranges in northern Iran. The composition of galbanum includes approximately 8% terpenes, about 65% resin containing sulfur, around 20% gum, and a very small amount of a colorless crystalline substance known as umbelliferone. Galbanum is one of the oldest known medicinal substances. It is mentioned in the Book of Exodus (30:34) as a sweet spice used in the preparation of a sacred perfume for the tabernacle. However, Rabbi Shelomo ben Yitschak (Rashi) in the 1100s noted that galbanum has a bitter quality and was included in the incense as a symbolic reminder of deliberate and unrepentant sinners. In modern times, galbanum is occasionally used in the production of perfumes. It is the ingredient responsible for the distinctive and unique scent of the fragrance Must by Cartier. Historically, Hippocrates utilized galbanum in medicine, and Pliny the Elder, in his Natural History (Book 24, Chapter 13), attributed remarkable healing properties to it. Pliny even claimed that merely touching galbanum mixed with oil of spodium was sufficient to kill a serpent. In contemporary medicine, galbanum is rarely prescribed, typically in doses ranging from five to fifteen grains. Its pharmacological actions are consistent with those of substances containing resin and volatile oils. However, its use in modern medical practice has largely fallen into obsolescence.
